newsitem.title: UK: UK to expand controversial welfare-to-work scheme.
newsitem.headline: UK to expand controversial welfare-to-work scheme.

text.p: Britain on Thursday announced plans to spend 100 million pounds ($164 million) on widening a controversial U.S.-style "workfare" scheme to try to get 100,000 long-term jobless back to work.

Education and Employment Secretary Gillian Shephard said she was extending "Project Work" to 29 areas after encouraging results in two towns that have piloted the scheme since April with 5,000 unemployed people.
"The latest indications are that around 25 percent more people are leaving the unemployment register than in comparable areas (without the schemes)," she said in a statement.

But the main opposition Labour party was critical, accusing the government of devising costly make-work schemes to keep the unemployment figures down in the run-up to the general election, which must be held by May.
Unemployment has fallen steadily in recent months and stood at 2.07 million, or 7.4 percent of the workforce, in September.
Under the programme, people aged 18 to 50 who have been out of work for more than two years are given 13 weeks of job-search training followed by 13 weeks of compulsory work experience.

As well as helping to wean the long-term unemployed off social security, the scheme aims to weed out fraudsters who have jobs but still claim welfare payments. Refusal to attend the work experience programmes can lead to benefits being halted.

Labour employment spokesman Stephen Byers said many of the 1,100 people in the two pilot schemes who had left the unemployment register had simply been shifted to other forms of welfare. Only one in 10 had got a job.

"We would support efforts to get people off the register who are defrauding the system, but they should not cloak it in a promotion that this is about new jobs for people. It clearly isn't that," Byers said.

Labour is proposing an alternative package of education and training aimed at shifting 250,000 under-25s off welfare and into work, financed by a windfall tax on the profits of privatised utilities. ($1=.6093 Pound)
